title: A Week Without Badges. What My Phone Stopped Demanding and I Stopped Missing
body: The red dot on the mail icon was not information. It was a standing order. I counted them one evening, every badge on every app, and the total was eleven. Eleven small red commands, each one saying the same sentence in a different font. Something here is unresolved, and you are the resolution. So the experiment. One week, every badge off. Every app. Not notifications, mind you, those came later. Just the badges, the counters, the dots. The phone would still buzz for calls and messages. Nothing would count anything at me. Day one was physiologically interesting. My thumb kept opening apps the way a tongue returns to a missing tooth. Open mail, nothing pending, close mail. The point was not that the mail was empty. The point was that I had been opening the mail to stop the dot, not to read the mail. The dot had turned a tool into a chore chart with me as the unpaid employee. Day two and three revealed the hierarchy. Without badges, I checked mail twice a day, at eleven and at four, in batches, like a person from history. Nobody noticed. The two things I had been afraid of, missing an urgent message and seeming unresponsive, both failed to materialize. Urgent things, it turns out, are defined by their channel, not by their badge. Real urgencies phone you. Day four was the relapse, worth recording honestly. A work group made me nervous, I re-enabled badges on one app at one in the afternoon, and by six I had checked it nine times and felt worse than on day one. The badge is not neutral technology. It is a leash with your name on it, and one hour of re-leashing undid four days of walking free. I turned it back off and noticed something else. The urge to re-enable came with a specific thought. What if something needs me. The accurate version of that thought is. What if something needs the version of me that is always interruptible. Those are different jobs, and I have been doing the second one without ever being hired for it. Days five to seven were quiet and I started finishing things. Whole tasks, end to end, without the micro-switching that badges had normalized. The badge system was training me, twenty times a day, to abandon whatever I was doing. That is its business model and it is very good at its business. After the week, the rules that survived. Badges stay off, permanently, on everything except the phone app and one messaging app, and even there I turned the count into a simple dot, presence without arithmetic. Notifications get batched to two daily deliveries for everything non-human. And one evening a week, the phone does a shift in a drawer, which started as a dramatic gesture and is now just Tuesday. The badge count on my phone is currently zero and has been for months. The strange part is that the world did not slow down and I did not become a monk. The same volume of mail arrives. The same groups chat. The difference is entirely about who counts. Something in the phone used to count my obligations for me, constantly, in red. Now the counting happens once, deliberately, on my schedule, by me. That is all the experiment was. Taking the abacus back from the machine. It was never heavy. I had just never noticed I was carrying it.
